title: When to Submit a 510(k): Use Readiness Gates Instead of a Calendar Target
description: Assess 510(k) readiness through intended use, predicate strategy, completed evidence, configuration control, and capacity to answer review questions.
intro: The best submission date is not necessarily the earliest date on which a dossier can be uploaded. A 510(k) is more likely to be coherent when the claim, device configuration, comparison, and supporting evidence are stable. A readiness review helps distinguish a genuinely complete package from one that depends on assumptions still being resolved.

sections.title: Stabilise the regulatory argument
paragraphs: Confirm the intended use, relevant device classification, and predicate strategy. FDA's 510(k) resources explain the substantial-equivalence framework; use that framework to identify the differences the submission must address. The commercial launch plan should reflect the claim actually supported by the evidence.

If a major pathway or study-design uncertainty remains, decide whether a focused regulatory interaction is appropriate before proceeding. Do not label an unresolved strategic question as a formatting task simply to keep the submission date unchanged.

sections.title: Check evidence and configuration together
paragraphs: For each important report, verify that the tested configuration represents the submitted device and that acceptance criteria support the relevant claim. Identify deviations, unresolved results, and subsequent design changes. A report's completion date is not enough to establish that it remains applicable.

Use a readiness table that separates completed evidence, justified exclusions, and open gaps. Identify dependencies such as final software, labelling, or manufacturing configuration. If a planned update changes the evidence basis soon after submission, evaluate whether it is more efficient to resolve it before filing.

sections.title: Plan the review period as active work
paragraphs: Reserve access to the engineers, clinical specialists, laboratory contacts, and document owners who may be needed to answer questions. Ensure that source records and analysis files are retrievable. A submission can be administratively complete while the team lacks the capacity to support it.

Set an internal response workflow with ownership, review, and cross-document consistency checks. Keep a controlled baseline of exactly what was submitted. Later answers should explain changes relative to that baseline rather than relying on an evolving folder in which the original version has disappeared.

example: A hypothetical team schedules filing immediately after a software test report is signed. A planned algorithm update will change the results presented in that report, and the final instructions are still being revised. A readiness gate exposes both dependencies. Management can then make an informed decision about timing instead of treating the signed report as evidence that the whole submission is ready.
checklist: Confirm intended use and predicate strategy.
Match reports to the submitted configuration.
Freeze and retain the submission baseline.

faq.question: Should a team wait until every future enhancement is complete?
faq.answer: No. Define a stable version and claim that the current evidence supports. Future enhancements can be managed separately through change control. The key is avoiding a submission whose own configuration or evidence remains unsettled.
